extracted.intended_audience: scholars, policymakers, lawyers, and citizens interested in administrative law, enforcement, and regulatory capture
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether and how enforcement decisions reflect regulatory capture: identifying who benefits, what decisions are affected, and what non-capture explanations might account for enforcement outcomes. The piece also considers reforms to limit discretionary power in enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify who is doing the capturing
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking to identify and understand regulatory capture, the important questions are who is doing the capturing, and what sort of decisions flow from the conquest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the regulated industry is always the captor; consider a range of actors (regulated entities, voters, future employers, staff, political patrons). The page emphasizes starting analysis by asking which actors exert influence over enforcement decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what sorts of decisions flow from capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on what sort of decisions flow from capture (e.g., bringing or declining to bring an enforcement action, resource allocation, adding or dropping charges, settlement choices, non-renewal or revocation of licenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine discrete enforcement choices across an enforcement portfolio—each involves discretion and can show distortions if systematically favoring particular interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat enforcement as a central component of administrative action
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement decisions are a major component of administrative action and are subject to the same pressures and practical problems as other executive functions, including formal prosecution and licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include enforcement contexts (prosecution, licensing agencies like the FCC, regulatory agencies like SEC or FTC) when analyzing capture; do not confine capture analysis to rulemaking or lobbying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider industry heterogeneity (industries are not monolithic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulated industries may be divided, with some firms pushing hard for enforcement while others prefer restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic 'industry capture' explanations; analyze intra-industry dynamics to see which firms benefit from a given enforcement choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for non-industry incentives shaping enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcers can gain favor for bringing actions (publicity, career advancement) and may act to impress voters, gain notoriety, secure support from staff, or follow their own ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate officials' career and reputational incentives (e.g., prosecutors as springboards to higher office, NAAG as 'National Association of Aspiring Governors') as alternative explanations for enforcement behavior that might otherwise be labeled capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess chance and contextual factors affecting enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular enforcement actions can be affected by chance (what cases are underway when a decision must be made, how one case fits with others, what resources are available in the budget at the time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish random or contingent influences from systematic bias; consider caseload timing, concurrent investigations, and budgetary cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate cost–benefit balancing by enforcers
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement officials have to balance the costs of an action against its expected benefit, which might be evaluated in terms of public interests or narrower interests of the official or agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize whether the benefit calculation is public-interest oriented or skewed toward private/political gains; look at resource expenditure vs likely impact when judging whether a decision reflects capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider probability of success and resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcers respond to the perceived probability of success: they may decline to pursue enforcement unlikely to prevail to avoid depleting scarce resources and emboldening noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an enforcement action is not taken, assess whether rational resource management explains the decision rather than capture; similarly, consider whether weak cases would add little marginal enforcement value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the multiplicity and discreteness of enforcement decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every enforcement portfolio comprehends a multitude of discrete decisions (bring action or not, allocate resources, add charges, compromise or drop actions), each with its own discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze patterns across many discrete choices rather than single cases to detect systematic favoring of particular interests indicative of capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the enormous scope and complexity of enforceable rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional laws and administrative rules are voluminous (e.g., thousands of rules and hundreds of thousands of pages of regulations), making nearly everyone a potential enforcement target and conferring huge discretionary power on enforcers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in how breadth and complexity of the regulatory state increase opportunities for discretion and potential capture; evaluate whether reducing rules would limit discretionary leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about inferring capture from questionable enforcement alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement decisions that appear questionable might reflect regulatory capture, but that is neither obvious nor easily encapsulated in a simple storyline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require careful analysis distinguishing capture from chance, administrative judgment, or legitimate prioritization before concluding that decisions are products of capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened scrutiny for enforcement decisions as a means to check capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement decisions merit heightened scrutiny if regulatory capture is to be reined in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus oversight attention on enforcement choices and the incentives shaping them; increased transparency and review of enforcement discretion can help detect bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy reform: pare back the range and complexity of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Paring back the range and complexity of the rules to be enforced is an excellent place to start to limit enforcers' discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a reform, reduce regulatory complexity to shrink enforcement discretion and potential avenues for capture; consider rule simplification as a structural remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include licensing enforcement as a distinct site of capture risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement in licensing contexts (e.g., FCC non-renewal or revocation of television and radio licenses) is an area where enforcement discretion can have profound effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing capture, examine licensing agencies and their use of renewal/non-renewal or revocation powers, since these are meaningful levers that can be influenced by special interests or political considerations.
